title: Lyra - Discovery: Migration from OpenAI to Dedicated
summary: Discovery call to understand Lyra Health's requirements for migrating from OpenAI-hosted endpoints to a dedicated/private Redwood deployment. Topics included compatibility with OpenAI API, eval parity, latency and cost tradeoffs, vLLM/TGI concerns, security (SOC2, KMS, SSO), and next steps for a pilot and benchmark run.
next_steps: Redwood to share dedicated sizing & pricing options (Alex)
SE to run compatibility checklist and sample shim for Lyra prompts (Morgan)
Lyra to share 2 representative prompt sets and eval metrics (Jordan)
Schedule benchmarking call next week to review initial numbers (all)
action_items: Alex Patel: Send Dedicated pricing sheet and example contracts (due: 2026-02-24)
Morgan Chen: Provide vLLM/TGI compatibility notes + sample shim repo link (due: 2026-02-23)
Jordan Lee: Upload 2 prompt sets and target eval scripts to shared drive (due: 2026-02-25)
Priya Nair: Share SOC2 questions and security contact for deeper review (due: 2026-02-24)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Patel (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Can you hear me okay?
[00:02] Sam Ortega (Lyra CTO): Yeah, all good. Thanks Alex.
[00:05] Jordan Lee (Lyra - Lead ML Eng): Morning, thanks. Excited to dig in.
[00:08] Alex Patel: Cool. Quick intros - I'm Alex, I'm the AE at Redwood working with healthcare accounts. Morgan, do you want to intro?
[00:15] Morgan Chen (Redwood SE): Sure, I'm Morgan, SE focused on inference and deployments, we work across Hosted, Dedicated and Private stacks.
[00:22] Priya Nair (Lyra - Security): Hi, I'm Priya, I handle security and compliance for Lyra.
[00:26] Tomi Alvarez (Lyra - Product): Tomi from Product; we'll be driving the success metrics.
[00:30] Alex Patel: Great. High level - Lyra's currently using OpenAI endpoints for a bunch of features, correct? Jordan can you summarize what specifically you're running in prod and what's motivating a migration?
[00:40] Jordan Lee: Yeah so in prod we have three main flows: clinical note summarization, patient messaging assistant, and a coding-assist feature for our internal cert team. We're hitting token limits and cost has been creeping. Also, some of our customers want data residency and more control - so we're evaluating Dedicated or Private.
[01:00] Morgan Chen: Understood. When you say OpenAI endpoints - is that direct OpenAI hosted API, or via another cloud partner like Azure?
[01:06] Jordan Lee: Direct OpenAI API. We tried Anthropic for a PoC but had quality regressions there.
[01:12] Sam Ortega: And to add, our compliance folks are pushing for SOC2 plus tighter key control. So KMS integration or HSM is a must for us.
[01:20] Alex Patel: Makes sense. A few typical migration questions we see: compatibility with your existing API calls, eval parity (i.e., are responses consistent when you move models/weights), latency & cost tradeoffs when moving to Dedicated, and whether open-source runtime choices like vLLM or TGI will be required.
[01:36] Jordan Lee: Right, about compatibility - we've got a bunch of wrapper logic around the OpenAI ChatCompletion API. We need something that doesn't force us to rewrite everything. Do you offer an OpenAI-compatible endpoint?
[01:45] Morgan Chen: Short answer: yes, we provide a compatibility layer. Longer answer: we support the common Chat/Completions/Embeddings shapes and can accept the same prompt/payload shapes; there are edge cases with streaming and function-calling where you may need a small shim. We typically provide sample client shims.
[02:00] Jordan Lee: Good. We also use streaming heavily for UX. Any caveats there?
[02:05] Morgan Chen: Streaming is supported in Hosted and Dedicated. For Dedicated, streaming latency depends on your instance sizing and batch settings. We can preserve chunked token stream semantics; sometimes slight differences occur because of batching windows - you'll see chunk granularity changes rather than semantic differences.
[02:22] Tomi Alvarez: You mentioned batch windows - does that mean latency could spike if you batch aggressively to save cost?
[02:27] Morgan Chen: Exactly. It's the classic latency vs cost tradeoff. We expose batching configs per route. If you're trying to keep 200ms p50 for short prompts, you'd pick minimal batching and reserve capacity accordingly. If you can tolerate 400-600ms, batching buys big token-cost reductions.
[02:43] Priya Nair: On the security side - can Dedicated use our KMS? We need customer-managed keys for model inputs/outputs at rest.
[02:51] Morgan Chen: Yes, Dedicated and Private deployments support customer KMS integration. For our Private on-prem you can use HSM/KMS, and for Dedicated we offer a KMS connector that integrates with AWS KMS or GCP/KMS depending on region. Audit logs and per-request metadata are also available.
[03:08] Sam Ortega: How about SSO? We use Okta and we need RBAC across teams.
[03:12] Alex Patel: We support SAML/SSO through our console and RBAC roles; for Dedicated we can sync with your IdP for team-level access. We'll share the SSO integration doc.
[03:20] Jordan Lee: Back to models - we need eval parity. Our current qualitative tests are sensitive; even small phrasing differences cause failed hallucination checks. If we move models, how can we ensure parity?
[03:32] Morgan Chen: Parity is tricky. We do two things: 1) model mapping and curated model variants - we recommend specific open models that approximate your OpenAI model, and 2) eval harnesses - we run your prompt sets against both Hosted and Dedicated builds to compare outputs and measure divergence on your metrics. We also offer rollback and can route a percentage to Hosted while you validate.
[03:52] Jordan Lee: Do you run the same tokenizer/version etc? We've seen tokenization shifts between runtimes that break our cost estimates.
[03:58] Morgan Chen: We try to match tokenization exactly where possible - our engine supports standard BPE/SentencePiece variants. If a custom tokenizer is a blocker, we can run pre-tokenization at your side and pass token counts. We'll surface any mismatch in the compatibility report.
[04:14] Tomi Alvarez: You mentioned vLLM and TGI earlier - what's the recommendation? We were evaluating vLLM for latency.
[04:20] Morgan Chen: vLLM and TGI are popular open-source runtimes. For low-latency single inference, vLLM is often better because of KV cache optimizations and attention kernels. However, vLLM can be more work to productionize at scale compared to Redwood's managed runtime which includes optimized kernels, batching, and fault-tolerant autoscaling. If you want to self-host and are comfortable maintaining the stack, vLLM/TGI are options; otherwise Dedicated gives many of the same perf wins with less ops.
[04:45] Jordan Lee: Any empirical numbers you can share? Sample p50/p95 for a 2k token context on an A100-like instance?
[04:53] Morgan Chen: We can share benchmark ranges: on a 1xA100 class node with optimized kernels we see generation latencies around 120-180ms p50 for short prompts, p95 depends heavily on sequence length; for 2k contexts you're looking more at 300-600ms p50 depending on model and quantization. But we'll run your prompts for an apples-to-apples comparison.
[05:15] Sam Ortega: Cost - we care about per-token unit economics. How does Dedicated pricing compare to Hosted?
[05:21] Alex Patel: Hosted is usage-based and simpler; Dedicated is committed capacity pricing (monthly/annual) that gives predictable throughput and lower per-token cost at scale. We'll share a few commitment tiers and sample cost curves based on your volume.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: We run a mix of high-volume short prompts and occasional long generations. Can Dedicated auto-scale for bursts?
[05:39] Morgan Chen: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity options. You can set a baseline reserved pool and allow bursts to shared capacity or additional nodes for a bounded period. For strict isolation we can set hard caps but then you need to provision for peak.
[05:55] Priya Nair: A security question - how are logs stored? We need to ensure PHI is not retained beyond our retention policy, and that access to logs is auditable.
[06:05] Morgan Chen: In Dedicated, logs are stored in your customer-controlled bucket or we can ship them to your SIEM. We support redaction options, encrypted-at-rest storage, and per-request audit metadata. For Private on-prem, logs never leave your network.
[06:20] Tomi Alvarez: About compatibility again - function calling is important for us. Any differences vs OpenAI's function calling?
[06:26] Morgan Chen: We support function calling semantics; there are minor differences in how suggestions for JSON schema are serialized. In practice we advise capturing results with a light parsing shim - we'll provide example code. Most customers only need a couple small tweaks.
[06:40] Jordan Lee: Great. On the eval side, we have an internal pass/fail with thresholds on hallucination and accuracy. Will you run the same metrics?
[06:47] Morgan Chen: Yes. We'll run your metrics and produce delta reports on the exact prompts. If regressions appear, we can test model variants (quantized 4-bit, int8, different open model weights) and also tune decoding params. We can run canary rollouts to check in prod without fully swapping.
[07:04] Alex Patel: One operational note - if we do a pilot, typical timeline is: share prompts & metrics, we run a 1-2 week benchmark on Dedicated, then a short pilot with a percentage of traffic, then broader migration. Does that timeline work?
[07:15] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's reasonable. We have a compliance review window for March so it'd be great to have numbers before then.
[07:22] Sam Ortega: Another thing - our engineering team experimented with a TGI-backed setup and saw memory pressure with long contexts. Does Redwood support model quantization to reduce memory?
[07:32] Morgan Chen: Yes. We recommend quantization profiles per workload. For example, q4/qlora-like profiles reduce memory and often keep quality acceptable. We provide model & quant recommendations as part of Optimize. For Dedicated we can deploy quantized variants and measure the quality tradeoffs on your evals.
[07:48] Tomi Alvarez: If we need to run some internal benchmarks first, what's the minimum info you need from us?
[07:54] Morgan Chen: Two representative prompt sets (short and long), target quality metrics and thresholds, token volumes (monthly/peak), and whether you require streaming/function-calls. Also region preference for latency.
[08:06] Jordan Lee: OK we'll gather that. Quick question - if we want to keep using OpenAI Hosted in parallel during validation, can you route a subset of traffic there?
[08:12] Alex Patel: Yes - Redwood's smart routing can split routes by percentage, region or latency policy. We can keep a shadow traffic pattern to Hosted until you're comfortable.
[08:22] Priya Nair: For legal - will you provide a standard DPA and SOC2 artifacts?
[08:26] Alex Patel: Yep, we have standard DPA templates and can share SOC2 Type II report. For Dedicated/Private we can provide architecture and dataflow docs.
[08:36] Jordan Lee: Anything we should watch out for in terms of hidden migration debt?
[08:40] Morgan Chen: Mainly tokenizer differences, slight decoding differences between model weights, and any custom prompt engineering that relied on OpenAI-specific quirks. Also client-side instrumentation: ensure you capture request IDs so you can correlate outputs in both systems.
[08:54] Sam Ortega: Sounds good. Can you also share a sample SLA for Dedicated? Our procurement team will need it.
[08:59] Alex Patel: We'll attach the SLA and contract examples in the follow-up email.
[09:04] Tomi Alvarez: For the pilot, we care about budget - what's a conservative estimate for a small pilot (say 3-4k requests/day with mixed prompt lengths)?
[09:13] Alex Patel: We'll put together sample pricing tiers with both hosted-equivalent cost and Dedicated committed tiers. Expect a pilot band that's higher on a per-unit basis than mature committed pricing but lower in management overhead than self-hosting. We'll include rough numbers in the follow-up.
[09:28] Morgan Chen: One more technical note - if you have custom tokenizers or private LLM fine-tunes, Dedicated can include those, but we need the artifacts early so we can bake them into the runtime.
[09:40] Jordan Lee: We do have a small fine-tune for the summarizer - we can share model artifacts.
[09:44] Priya Nair: We'll need to validate the model handling process for IP controls.
[09:48] Morgan Chen: Understood. We'll document the model onboarding workflow and admin controls.
[09:54] Alex Patel: Alright let's recap next steps. We'll: 1) Alex sends pricing, SLA and DPA; 2) Morgan sends compatibility checklist and sample shim repo; 3) Lyra shares prompt sets and metrics; 4) schedule benchmark run for next week. Anything else?
[10:10] Jordan Lee: That covers it. Also can you include any public benchmark docs you've done versus vLLM/TGI? Those help with our engineering review.
[10:17] Morgan Chen: Yes, I'll include a perf appendix and notes about quantization tradeoffs.
[10:22] Sam Ortega: Thank you all.
[10:24] Alex Patel: Thanks team - we'll follow up.
[10:27] [Meeting ends]
